title: Month-over-month change

WITH m AS (
    SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS MonthStart,
           SUM(EstimatedValue) AS Total
    FROM brokerage.TradeOrders
    GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1)

SELECT MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart)         AS PrevMonth,
       Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart) AS Change
FROM m
ORDER BY MonthStart;

WITH t AS (
    SELECT p.Region, p.AccountName, SUM(e.EstimatedValue) AS TotalEstimatedValue,

)

FROM t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY Region, rn;

title: Monthly rank of securities

WITH m AS (
    SELECT MONTH(e.OrderDate) AS MonthNo, d.SecurityName, SUM(e.EstimatedValue) AS Total,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY MONTH(e.OrderDate) ORDER BY SUM(e.EstimatedValue) DESC) AS rnk

    JOIN brokerage.Securities AS d ON d.SecurityID = e.SecurityID
    GROUP BY MONTH(e.OrderDate), d.SecurityID, d.SecurityName
)

FROM m
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY MonthNo;

title: Repeat trade orders within N days
q: Find trade orders that happened within @Days days of the same account's previous trade order. Use @Days = 145. Show account, previous date, current date and gap.
sql:
DECLARE @Days int = 145;

WITH v AS (
    SELECT AccountID, OrderID, OrderDate,
           LAG(OrderDate) OVER (PARTITION BY AccountID ORDER BY OrderDate, OrderID) AS PrevDate
    FROM brokerage.TradeOrders
)
SELECT AccountID, PrevDate, OrderDate,
       DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, OrderDate) AS GapDays
FROM v
WHERE PrevDate IS NOT NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, OrderDate) <= @Days
ORDER BY AccountID, OrderDate;

title: Constraint vs trigger vs app
q: Write a query that shows, for each table, how many PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints it has.
sql:
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS TableName,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'PK' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS PK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'F'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'UQ' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS UQ,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'C'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS CK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'D'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DF
FROM sys.objects
WHERE type IN ('PK', 'F', 'UQ', 'C', 'D')
  AND SCHEMA_NAME(schema_id) = 'brokerage'
GROUP BY parent_object_id
ORDER BY TableName;
how: Prefer declarative constraints: they are faster, always applied, and help the optimizer. Use triggers only for cross-table rules, and application checks for friendly messages.

q: Starting from account 1's first trade order, use a recursive CTE to walk forward through that account's trade orders in date order, with a step number.

WITH Ordered AS (
    SELECT OrderID, OrderDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate, OrderID) AS rn
    FROM brokerage.TradeOrders
    WHERE AccountID = 1
), Chain AS (
    SELECT OrderID, OrderDate, rn, 0 AS Step
    FROM Ordered
    WHERE rn = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.OrderID, o.OrderDate, o.rn, c.Step + 1
    FROM Ordered AS o
    JOIN Chain AS c ON o.rn = c.rn + 1
)

FROM Chain
ORDER BY Step;

title: MAXRECURSION
q: Generate numbers 1 to 200 with a recursive CTE. (The default limit is 100 levels.)
sql:
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 200
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS HowMany, MAX(n) AS LastNumber
FROM N
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 200);

title: Month-over-month with a calendar

    SELECT mo.m, ISNULL(SUM(e.EstimatedValue), 0) AS Total
    FROM Months AS mo
    LEFT JOIN brokerage.TradeOrders AS e
           ON e.OrderDate >= mo.m AND e.OrderDate < DATEADD(month, 1, mo.m)

       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS PrevTotal,
       CAST(100.0 * (Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m))

title: Org-chart style hierarchy with path
q: Build a small hierarchy in a table variable (region head > team > account) and list it with a recursive CTE, showing each level and a path like Head > North > Olivia.
sql:
DECLARE @Org TABLE (NodeID int, ParentID int NULL, NodeName nvarchar(100));
INSERT INTO @Org VALUES (0, NULL, N'Head');
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Region), 0, Region
FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts
GROUP BY Region;
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT 100 + p.AccountID, r.NodeID, p.AccountName
FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts AS p
JOIN @Org AS r ON r.NodeName = p.Region
WHERE p.AccountID <= 6;

WITH Tree AS (
    SELECT NodeID, NodeName, 0 AS Lvl, CAST(NodeName AS nvarchar(400)) AS PathText
    FROM @Org
    WHERE ParentID IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.NodeID, o.NodeName, t.Lvl + 1,
           CAST(t.PathText + N' > ' + o.NodeName AS nvarchar(400))
    FROM @Org AS o
    JOIN Tree AS t ON o.ParentID = t.NodeID
)
SELECT NodeID, Lvl, PathText
FROM Tree
ORDER BY PathText;

title: MERGE: sync a staging table
q: Sync account regions from a staging list: update regions that changed, insert new accounts, and report each action.
sql:
DECLARE @Stage TABLE (AccountID int, AccountName nvarchar(80), AccountNumber varchar(20), Region varchar(10));
INSERT INTO @Stage
SELECT AccountID, AccountName, AccountNumber, CASE WHEN Region = 'East' THEN 'West' ELSE 'East' END
FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts WHERE AccountID = 1          -- region change
UNION ALL
SELECT AccountID, AccountName, AccountNumber, Region
FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts WHERE AccountID = 2          -- no change
UNION ALL
SELECT 301, N'New BrokerageAccount', '82010000000301', 'North';     -- new

MERGE brokerage.BrokerageAccounts AS t
USING @Stage AS s
   ON t.AccountID = s.AccountID
WHEN MATCHED AND t.Region <> s.Region THEN
    UPDATE SET t.Region = s.Region
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (AccountID, AccountName, AccountNumber, Region, ClientID)
    VALUES (s.AccountID, s.AccountName, s.AccountNumber, s.Region, 1)
OUTPUT $action AS ActionTaken, inserted.AccountID, deleted.Region AS OldRegion, inserted.Region AS NewRegion;
how: MERGE does insert, update and (optionally) delete in one statement. The extra `AND t.Region <> s.Region` skips rows that did not change. $action in OUTPUT reports what happened to each row.

title: Generate test rows with a set
q: Insert 20 test trade orders for account 1 in one statement, one per day starting 2025-01-01, with IDs 1001-1020.
sql:
WITH N AS (
    SELECT TOP (20) ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)) AS n
    FROM sys.all_objects
)
INSERT INTO brokerage.TradeOrders
    (OrderID, AccountID, OrderReference, RoutingCategory, WorkflowStatus, EstimatedValue,
     RequestedQuantity, OrderDate, SubmittedAt, RecordedAt, SecurityID)
SELECT 1000 + n, 1, CONCAT(N'BRO-TEST-', n), 'A', 'Open', 100, 1,
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01' AS date)),
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01 09:00' AS datetime2(3))),
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01 09:01 +00:00' AS datetimeoffset(3))), 1
FROM N;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS TestRows, MIN(OrderDate) AS FirstDate, MAX(OrderDate) AS LastDate
FROM brokerage.TradeOrders
WHERE OrderID BETWEEN 1001 AND 1020;

title: Isolation levels
q: Name SQL Server's transaction isolation levels and the problem each one prevents. Show the current level.
sql:
SELECT CASE transaction_isolation_level
         WHEN 1 THEN 'READ UNCOMMITTED' WHEN 2 THEN 'READ COMMITTED'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'REPEATABLE READ'  WHEN 4 THEN 'SERIALIZABLE'
         WHEN 5 THEN 'SNAPSHOT' END AS IsolationLevel
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE session_id = @@SPID;
how: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED (the default) prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE also prevents phantom rows. SNAPSHOT reads a consistent version without blocking writers. Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more blocking.

title: Joins that multiply rows
q: Show each account's total trade order estimated value and total number of executions. Make sure the estimated value is not double counted.
sql:
SELECT p.AccountID, p.AccountName,
       ISNULL(ch.TotalEstimatedValue, 0) AS TotalEstimatedValue,
       ISNULL(li.Executions, 0) AS Executions
FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts AS p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT AccountID, SUM(EstimatedValue) AS TotalEstimatedValue
           FROM brokerage.TradeOrders
           GROUP BY AccountID) AS ch ON ch.AccountID = p.AccountID
LEFT JOIN (SELECT e.AccountID, COUNT(*) AS Executions
           FROM brokerage.Executions AS r
           JOIN brokerage.TradeOrders AS e ON e.OrderID = r.OrderID
           GROUP BY e.AccountID) AS li ON li.AccountID = p.AccountID
ORDER BY TotalEstimatedValue DESC;
how: If you join TradeOrders and Executions first and then SUM(EstimatedValue), a trade order with 2 executions has its estimated value counted twice (fan-out). Aggregating each child table separately before joining fixes this. Interviewers often test whether you spot fan-out.

title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
q: Interview trap: show why NOT IN fails when the list contains NULL. Find trade orders that are not a parent of any other trade order, first with NOT IN (wrong), then with NOT EXISTS (right).
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM brokerage.TradeOrders AS e
   WHERE e.OrderID NOT IN (SELECT ParentOrderID
                               FROM brokerage.TradeOrders)) AS NotIn_Wrong,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM brokerage.TradeOrders AS e
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM brokerage.TradeOrders AS c
                     WHERE c.ParentOrderID = e.OrderID)) AS NotExists_Right;
how: ParentOrderID is NULL on every row here. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so NOT IN returns 0. NOT EXISTS ignores the NULLs and correctly finds that no trade order is a parent. You can also fix NOT IN by adding `WHERE ParentOrderID IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

title: Top account per region
q: Using only subqueries (no window functions), show the account with the highest total estimated value in each region.
sql:
SELECT t.Region, t.AccountName, t.Total
FROM (SELECT p.Region, p.AccountName, SUM(e.EstimatedValue) AS Total
      FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts AS p
      JOIN brokerage.TradeOrders AS e ON e.AccountID = p.AccountID
      GROUP BY p.Region, p.AccountID, p.AccountName) AS t
WHERE t.Total = (SELECT MAX(t2.Total)
                 FROM (SELECT p2.Region, SUM(e2.EstimatedValue) AS Total
                       FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts AS p2
                       JOIN brokerage.TradeOrders AS e2 ON e2.AccountID = p2.AccountID
                       GROUP BY p2.Region, p2.AccountID) AS t2
                 WHERE t2.Region = t.Region)
ORDER BY t.Region;

title: Trade orders after an account's first execution
q: For each account who has an execution, count how many of their trade orders happened after the trade order of their first execution.
sql:
SELECT x.AccountID, COUNT(e.OrderID) AS LaterTradeOrders
FROM (SELECT e1.AccountID, MIN(e1.OrderDate) AS FirstRxDate
      FROM brokerage.Executions AS li
      JOIN brokerage.TradeOrders AS e1 ON e1.OrderID = li.OrderID
      GROUP BY e1.AccountID) AS x
LEFT JOIN brokerage.TradeOrders AS e
       ON e.AccountID = x.AccountID
      AND e.OrderDate > x.FirstRxDate
GROUP BY x.AccountID
ORDER BY LaterTradeOrders DESC, x.AccountID;
how: The derived table finds each account's first execution date. The LEFT JOIN on a date condition counts the later trade orders, and accounts with none get 0.

title: IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN
q: Return accounts with at least one Pending trade order three ways (IN, EXISTS, JOIN with DISTINCT). Each should return the same count.
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts
   WHERE AccountID IN (SELECT AccountID FROM brokerage.TradeOrders
                       WHERE WorkflowStatus = 'Pending')) AS ViaIn,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts AS p
   WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM brokerage.TradeOrders AS e
                 WHERE e.AccountID = p.AccountID AND e.WorkflowStatus = 'Pending')) AS ViaExists,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.AccountID)
   FROM brokerage.BrokerageAccounts AS p
   JOIN brokerage.TradeOrders AS e ON e.AccountID = p.AccountID
   WHERE e.WorkflowStatus = 'Pending') AS ViaJoin;
how: All three give the same answer. A plain JOIN repeats an account for each matching trade order, which is why DISTINCT is needed. IN and EXISTS never duplicate rows.

title: Above their group's average
q: List trade orders whose estimated value is more than the average estimated value of their own trade order type.
sql:
SELECT e.OrderID, e.RoutingCategory, e.EstimatedValue
FROM brokerage.TradeOrders AS e
WHERE e.EstimatedValue > (SELECT AVG(x.EstimatedValue) FROM brokerage.TradeOrders AS x
                  WHERE x.RoutingCategory = e.RoutingCategory)
ORDER BY e.RoutingCategory, e.EstimatedValue DESC, e.OrderID;
how: The correlated subquery calculates the average for the current row's type. AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the window-function alternative.
